The absence of prodromal symptoms 1–2 weeks prior makes classic viral exanthems like parvovirus B19 (which typically has a 5–14 day prodrome with fever/malaise before rash) less likely, though not impossible. Guttate psoriasis is highly plausible: it commonly follows streptococcal infection (though not always recalled), presents with small, scaly, pruritic papules/plaques starting in flexures and spreading widely, and is associated with arthralgias (psoriatic arthritis can be subclinical early on); the acute febrile and arthralgic onset fits. Pityriasis rosea is also strong: classically begins with a herald patch (often missed), then spreads with bilateral, symmetric, oval, collarette-scaly lesions, frequently involving trunk and proximal limbs; pruritus and mild constitutional symptoms (low-grade fever, arthralgia) occur in ~25% of cases; absence of joint swelling aligns. AGEP is considered due to rapid onset, fever, and widespread rash — but lacks characteristic non-follicular sterile pustules on exam (not described, so lower confidence). Parvovirus B19 is downgraded because no prodrome and atypical distribution (fifth disease usually starts on face/cheeks with 'slapped cheek' and spares flexures early); however, atypical presentations occur. DRESS is less likely given short duration (typically >2–3 weeks after drug initiation), absence of lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, or organ involvement (e.g., hepatitis, nephritis) — but cannot be fully excluded without medication history or labs.
